transcript.content: Hi, welcome in. I'm Dr. Lee. To start, can you tell me what's been going on that brought you in today?

Well, Dr. Lee... mostly I just don't feel like myself anymore. I don't know. I stopped doing everything. I stopped hiking, coaching... I used to coach this youth team, and we had this one kid who always brought these orange slices that his mom cut up into little triangles. She worked at the hardware store, I think. Good people. They had a golden retriever that would run onto the field. But I don't do that now. 

I stopped playing my guitar, too. I don't even call people back. Some days I just sit in that small rental for hours. It's a really tight space, the rental, right near the highway so you hear the trucks going by all night. The 18-wheelers always sound louder when it rains, you know? The water on the asphalt makes this hissing sound that just goes on and on. 

But... yeah, I just sit there. I know there are things to do, like chores or whatever, but I just can't make myself start.
How long have you been feeling this way—weeks, months, or longer?

It's been... months. Actually, about a year and two months ago. That's when things really started unraveling. I had to move into that smaller rental right after my divorce. 

Packing up all our stuff took forever. We had this huge collection of vinyl records. My ex-wife loved jazz, especially the old stuff with the scratchy audio. We bought this antique record player at a flea market in... I think it was Springfield. The guy selling it had a glass eye. You could tell because it didn't move when he looked at you, it just stayed fixed on the horizon. He told us he lost it in a fishing accident, which doesn't make a lot of sense if you really think about it. How do you lose an eye fishing? Unless the hook caught the wind and whipped back around, maybe. I used to go fishing with my uncle on this lake that was so clear you could see the rocks at the bottom. 

I used to listen to those jazz records after my patrol shifts, just take off my boots and sit there in the dark. But... yeah, a year and two months. Since the divorce.
Have you ever heard voices or sounds that others couldn't hear, or felt that people were watching you or trying to harm you in ways that others didn't believe were true?

Voices? Well... I mean, I hear the radio. My scanner. Even when it's completely turned off and just sitting on the kitchen counter, I hear it. It's one of those older, heavy-duty models with the thick rubber antenna. My old partner, Dave, he used to chew on the end of his antenna during night shifts. Completely ruined the casing. Dave had this weird habit of eating sunflower seeds and spitting the shells into a paper cup, but he'd always miss, and they'd end up in the cruiser's cup holder. It drove me crazy because they'd get all sticky with spilled coffee. He drank his coffee black, but he always bought it from this gas station that burned the beans. 

Anyway, the scanner... it's off, but I still hear these short, static-y bursts coming from it. Like dispatch, but it's not dispatch. It's these voices, and they're usually warning me. They tell me that someone is inside the house, or that I'm being watched right that second. 

And I know how to clear a building, right? I do it by the book. I take my flashlight—the heavy Maglite that takes four D batteries. You can't even buy D batteries at the corner store anymore, you have to go all the way to the big box store on Route 9, and the one near me always smells like fertilizer because the garden center is right by the entrance. They had a massive sale on mulch last week, bags piled up to the ceiling. But I use the flashlight and I clear every single room in that rental. Every closet, under the bed, checking the corners. But even after I've cleared every room and I know nobody is there... I'll still see this shadow. Just sliding past the hallway wall, right out of the corner of my eye.
Have you noticed whether these voices and shadow-like visions only happen when you're feeling really down and low, or do they also occur during times when your mood feels okay?

When I feel okay? I... I don't really know. I haven't kept track of that. I guess I haven't really felt "okay" in a long time anyway, so it's hard to compare. 

I used to feel okay when I'd take my patrol cruiser through the automatic car wash at the end of my shift, though. The one on 5th Street. The guys at the precinct always gave me grief because I'd pay out of pocket for the premium wash with that tri-color foam. It sprayed pink, blue, and yellow all over the windshield, and it smelled exactly like artificial cherry. Like those hard cough drops my grandmother used to keep wrapped in tissues in her purse. She had this heavy leather purse with a brass snap-clasp that sounded almost like a small caliber gunshot when she closed it. Real thick, heavy leather. You just don't see craftsmanship like that anymore, everything is synthetic now. I bought a synthetic winter coat last November and the zipper teeth misaligned on the very second day I wore it. You try to fix it, but once the plastic bends, it's just ruined. 

But... wait, what were you asking? About the shadows? I don't really know when they happen.
Did you start hearing these scanner voices and seeing the shadow before you began feeling depressed, or did they start around the same time as the low mood?

Before or same time? I... I'm not really sure which came first. It all just sort of bleeds together now. I used to keep track of everything, every little detail, in this tiny spiral notebook. A pocket one, you know? Fits right in the breast pocket of the uniform. 

The spiral wire on those things always used to catch on the fabric, though, and it would pull these little blue threads out. My ex-wife hated when I brought those shirts home to wash because the threads would tangle up in the machine. We had this old top-loading washer that sounded exactly like a helicopter taking off during the spin cycle. The repair guy said the drum was unbalanced, but he charged eighty bucks just to walk through the door and look at it. Eighty bucks! And he tracked mud all over the kitchen linoleum. It was that sticky, red clay kind of mud. You only really see that specific kind of clay out past the county line near the old brickyard. 

We had a call out there once, some kids trespassing, and my boots were covered in that red clay for a week. The tread on those tactical boots is so deep, it's basically impossible to clean out. You have to use a toothpick or a flathead screwdriver to dig the dried mud out of the grooves. I lost my favorite flathead screwdriver doing that. It had a yellow handle... 

But, I'm sorry, the timeline. Yeah, I couldn't tell you. I really don't know if the low mood started before the scanner voices or not. It's just all happening.

Thinking back over the past year, has there ever been a stretch of time—even just a week or two—when your mood felt normal or better, but you were still hearing the scanner voices or seeing that shadow?

Normal or better? I... I don't know. Like I said, I haven't really felt normal in a long time. So I can't really say if there was a week or two where I felt fine but still heard the scanner. It's just always there. 

You know, the scanner used to sit right next to this old coffee maker I had. A standard drip machine, nothing fancy. But it had this warming plate that would scorch the bottom of the pot if you left it on too long. It made the whole kitchen smell like burnt toast and old pennies. I tried to clean the burnt stains off the glass with baking soda and vinegar once. My mother swore by baking soda for everything. She used to keep an open box in the back of the refrigerator to absorb odors. Always the yellow box. I think they still make it the exact same way. But she'd forget to change it, so the box would just sit there for years, getting hard as a rock. You could probably use it as a doorstop. 

We had a heavy iron doorstop at the precinct, shaped like a bulldog. Some rookie tripped over it once and nearly broke his ankle. He had to wear this clunky walking boot for six weeks, and it squeaked every time he took a step on the linoleum. Squeak, squeak, squeak. Drove everyone insane. He ended up transferring out to a different district... 

Anyway, I don't really know about the weeks or the mood. I just... I don't have a good answer for that.
Going back further than the past year—say, two or three years ago, before your divorce—did you ever hear those scanner-like voices or see the shadow, even when you were feeling completely fine?

Before the divorce? Two or three years ago? I... I really couldn't tell you. It's so hard to remember what "fine" even felt like back then. Everything just kind of blends together. 

I do remember the day she left, though. She packed all her things into these cardboard boxes we got from the liquor store down the street. The ones with the dividers inside for the wine bottles. You have to pull those cardboard dividers out if you want to fit anything bigger than a pair of shoes in them. I used one of those dividers to organize my socket wrenches in the garage, actually. It worked pretty well until the humidity got to it and the cardboard got all soft and warped. 

Garages always get so damp in the summer. We had this dehumidifier out there, but you had to remember to empty the little plastic bucket every two days or it would shut off automatically. It had this little red float inside, kind of like the bobber you use for fishing. I haven't been fishing since I was a kid. My dad used to take me out to Miller's Pond, and we'd sit on these aluminum folding chairs that would get blisteringly hot in the sun. If you wore shorts, the backs of your thighs would just roast...

But, sorry, what were you asking? Before the divorce? Yeah, I don't know. I can't remember if I heard the voices or saw the shadow back then when I was feeling okay. I just don't know.
Right now, as we're sitting here talking, are you hearing the scanner voices or seeing the shadow at this very moment?

Right now? Well, no, not right this exact second. It's usually when I'm at home. I'll have the scanner turned completely off, you know, because sometimes you just need quiet after a shift. But even with it off, I hear these... short bursts. Like radio chatter. It's usually warning me, telling me someone is inside the house or that I'm being watched. And then there's the shadow. I'll see it move past the hallway, just out of the corner of my eye. I'll clear every room, check all the closets, behind the doors—standard procedure. You always check behind the doors because that's a blind spot. 

We learned that at the academy. They set up these mock rooms with cardboard cutouts of bad guys. If you didn't check the corner behind the door, the instructor would blow an air horn right in your ear. My ears rang for three days after my first room-clearing drill. The instructor, Sergeant Miller, he had this thick mustache that completely covered his upper lip. Reminded me of a walrus. He used to chew on these wooden matchsticks all day long. He'd just roll them from one side of his mouth to the other. I tried doing that once with a toothpick, but I accidentally bit down on it and got a splinter stuck right in my gums. Took me half an hour in front of the bathroom mirror with tweezers to get it out. Tweezers are so hard to grip when your hands are wet. I had just washed my hands with that cheap pink soap they have in public restrooms. It always smells like artificial cherries...

But, no, I'm not hearing them right now in your office. It's mostly at home, like I said. The warnings and the shadow in the hall.
Aside from low motivation, can you tell me how your sleep and appetite have been over the past couple of months—are you sleeping and eating more or less than usual?

Sleep and appetite? I don't know, I haven't really been paying attention to either of those things. I guess they're just... normal? I don't really know what normal is anymore, but I haven't noticed any big changes. 

I usually just eat whatever is easy. Canned soup, mostly. Chicken noodle. But you have to be careful with the pull-tab cans. I sliced my thumb open on one of those lids a few years back. The cut was so clean I didn't even feel it at first, just saw the blood dripping onto the linoleum. It was a pain to clean up. I had to use bleach, and the smell of bleach always reminds me of the community pool I went to as a kid. 

They used so much chlorine in that pool, your eyes would burn for hours after you got out. My mom used to make me wear these tight, neon green swim trunks. They had a little mesh lining inside that was incredibly uncomfortable. I always tried to cut it out with scissors, but I'd just end up fraying the edges. We had these heavy, dull scissors with orange plastic handles. They couldn't cut through anything thicker than a piece of paper. My dad used them to trim his mustache, which never made any sense to me. He had a really thick mustache, kind of like Sergeant Miller, actually. But my dad's was always a little lopsided. 

Anyway, I don't think my sleep or eating has changed much. Just the usual, I guess.
Has there ever been a stretch of at least a month, at any point, when you did not hear the scanner voices or see the shadow at all?

A whole month without them? No, no, it's been pretty constant lately. The voices, those shadows, and that feeling—that absolute certainty that people are tracking me—it's been going on for about four months now. Every single day for four months. 

Four months ago was October, right around Halloween. I always hated Halloween when I was on patrol. Kids running out into the street in dark costumes, teenagers smashing pumpkins... I remember one year, this kid threw a pumpkin off an overpass and it hit a patrol car. Smashed the windshield right in. The glass safety film held it together, though. That film is incredible stuff. They use something similar on the windows of banks, you know, to stop bullets. Or at least slow them down. I had to go to the bank last week to get a cashier's check, and they had these new pens chained to the desks. The chains were made of those little metal beads, like the ones on dog tags. I still have my dad's dog tags in a cigar box somewhere. The box smells like cedar and old tobacco. It's a nice smell. Not like the smell of burning leaves, which always makes my throat itch. My neighbor burns his leaves every fall, even though there's a city ordinance against it. I should probably report him, but... 

What was I saying? Oh, right. Yeah, four months. It hasn't stopped for a whole month at all. Just four months of it, straight through.

Thinking about the time between your divorce and about four months ago—before the scanner voices and shadow started—did the low mood and loss of interest stay the same the whole time, or was there any stretch where you felt more like your old self during those months?

Between the divorce and... four months ago? I don't know, it's hard to say. I guess it was just the same. Just that heavy feeling, not wanting to do anything. I don't remember feeling like my old self at all. 

My old self used to love fishing. I had this great little aluminum boat, a 14-footer. Perfect for getting into the shallows where the bass like to hide. The guy I bought it from had painted it this awful camouflage pattern, but he used interior house paint, so it started flaking off the first time I took it out. Little green and brown chips floating in the water. It looked like fish food, actually. I tried feeding fish in a pond once with breadcrumbs, but I read later that bread is terrible for them. It swells up in their stomachs. You're supposed to give them peas instead. Frozen peas, thawed out. My ex-wife used to put frozen peas on her eyes when she had a headache. She said the cold helped with the swelling, but I always thought she just looked ridiculous lying on the couch with vegetables on her face. She bought the generic brand peas, too. The bag always had more ice crystals than actual peas. Ice crystals remind me of the frost that builds up on the inside of my freezer. I need to defrost it, but it's such a hassle. You have to take everything out, put it in coolers... 

But yeah, no. I don't think there was any stretch where I felt better. Just the same low mood the whole time.

When you're feeling a bit less down—even just slightly better than usual—do you still fully believe that someone is in the house or watching you, with the same certainty as when you're feeling very low?

Even if I feel a little better, the mood doesn't change what's actually happening. I know it sounds extreme, but for months I've been certain the guys across from my rental and some people at work were tracking my patrol routes and testing my locks. The same cars and little comments kept lining up too perfectly to be random. It's not a feeling, it's just a fact. 

Speaking of locks, I had to replace the deadbolt on my front door last week. The old one was getting sticky, you know? You had to jiggle the key just right to get it to turn. It was one of those brass ones that tarnishes really easily. I tried polishing it once with this stuff I bought at the hardware store, but it smelled like rotten eggs. Sulfur, I guess. My high school chemistry teacher, Mr. Henderson, he used to do this demonstration with sulfur where he'd burn it in a fume hood. The flame was this beautiful, eerie blue color. Blue is my favorite color, actually. Like a deep navy blue, not that bright sky blue. Navy blue looks more professional. That's why most police uniforms are navy blue. It commands respect. Or at least it used to. Nowadays, people don't respect the uniform like they used to. They just see a target. 

But anyway, no, my mood doesn't change the facts. They're still tracking me.
Have you ever had a period—even just a few days—where you felt unusually energetic, elated, or irritable, needed much less sleep than usual but didn't feel tired, or felt like you could do anything?

No, no, I've never had anything like that. Unusually energetic? No. I mean, my energy is just gone most of the time. I definitely need my sleep, even if it's hard to get. 

Speaking of sleep, I used to have this incredible mattress. It was one of those memory foam ones, you know? But not the cheap kind that traps all your body heat so you wake up sweating. It had this cooling gel layer infused right into the top. I bought it on sale during a Labor Day weekend event. Labor Day sales are usually a scam, but this one was actually a good deal. They threw in two free pillows, too. The pillows were a little too firm for my liking, honestly. I ended up giving them to my brother. He loves firm pillows. He says they align his spine better. He's a chiropractor, so I guess he'd know. He works out of this little office in a strip mall next to a dry cleaner. The dry cleaner always smells like perchloroethylene. It's a sweet, chemical smell. I read an article once about how that stuff can get into the groundwater if they aren't careful with it. Groundwater contamination is a huge issue. There was this town in California where the water was so bad, people were getting sick just from taking showers... 

But, uh, what were you asking? Oh, feeling elated or needing less sleep? No, never had that. Just tired.

Doctor: Have you ever had a time where you experienced something really traumatic or life-threatening, and since then, you find yourself constantly on edge, easily startled, or having nightmares or flashbacks about it?

Patient: Traumatic? No, not really. I mean, the divorce was awful, but not life-threatening. I don't have flashbacks or anything like that. Just... normal bad memories, I guess. 

Memories are strange, aren't they? Like how you can remember the exact smell of a place from twenty years ago. My grandfather's garage always smelled like motor oil and sawdust. He used to build these intricate birdhouses out of scrap wood. He painted one bright red, like a fire engine. Fire engines are so loud, you know? The sirens just pierce right through you. I saw one responding to a call last week. It was one of those massive ladder trucks, trying to navigate a tight corner downtown. The driver had to back up twice just to make the turn. It's a tough job, driving something that big. My cousin drives an 18-wheeler. He hauls produce from Florida up to New York. He says the worst part is the boredom on those long stretches of highway in the Carolinas. Just trees and more trees. He listens to audiobooks to stay awake. Mostly thrillers, John Grisham kind of stuff. I tried listening to an audiobook once, but the narrator's voice was too soothing. I kept nodding off in my chair. It was a leather chair, too, so it got really hot if you sat in it too long. Real leather, not that bonded stuff that peels after a year...

But no, to answer your question, no traumatic events or flashbacks or being on edge like that. Just the scanner voices.
Right now, would you say your low mood and lack of interest have actually gotten a little better compared to a few months ago, even though the scanner voices and shadow are still just as strong?

Better? No, I wouldn't say that. Mostly I just don't feel like myself anymore. I used to do things, you know? But I completely stopped hiking, stopped coaching, even stopped playing my guitar. I haven't touched it in forever. It's an acoustic, a Martin. Really rich tone. My dad taught me a few chords when I was a kid. He used to listen to all those old folk records on vinyl. Vinyl is making a huge comeback, which is funny because I remember when everyone was throwing their records away to buy CDs. CDs get scratched so easily, though. You leave one in your car on a hot day, and it's ruined. Cars get like ovens in the summer. I used to patrol this one corporate parking lot where the asphalt would literally get soft in July. You could see your boot prints in it. It's terrible for your tires, too. Tires are so expensive now, and I really need to get my alignment checked because my truck pulls a little to the right when I hit the brakes... 

But, um, anyway. What I mean is, I stopped calling people back, too. Some days I just sit in that small rental for hours. I'll just sit there, knowing there are things I need to do—laundry, cleaning, whatever—but I just can't make myself start. So, no, the mood isn't really better.

I'm sorry, did you ask another question? I kind of drifted off there for a second. I was looking at the camera in the corner of your ceiling. Is that a closed-circuit system? 

I used to monitor those all the time when I worked security at the data center. We had over two hundred cameras on site. You had to watch these massive banks of monitors, and

...and you just get so hypnotized staring at all those little screens. Your eyes start playing tricks on you after a few hours. The glare is terrible, especially with the fluorescent lights we had in that control room. They had this constant, low hum, kind of like a refrigerator. Actually, the fridge in my rental has been making this awful grinding noise lately. I think the condenser fan is going out. I tried to pull it away from the wall to look at it, but the coils were just caked in this thick layer of dust. Dust is mostly dead skin cells, you know, which is pretty disgusting if you really think about it. No matter how much you clean, it just keeps coming back. I used to buy those yellow microfiber cloths in bulk from the auto parts store to keep my truck dashboard clean... but, wait, I'm sorry. I completely lost my train of thought. What did you just ask me? I don't think I heard you.

I'm sorry, did you ask a question? I was just looking at that pen you're holding. Is that a Parker? My grandfather had a whole collection of fountain pens in this felt-lined wooden box. He used to write these long letters in cursive to people he served with in the Navy. Nobody writes in cursive anymore, do they? They don't even teach it in schools. Everything is just typing and texting. I read somewhere that texting is ruining people's posture because they're always looking down at their phones, which puts like sixty pounds of pressure on your cervical spine. That's probably why my neck always hurts, honestly. I need to get a new pillow, maybe one of those memory foam ones. But anyway... what were you saying?

I'm not really sure. I haven't noticed anything like that, to be honest. It's hard to pay attention to stuff like that when... well, look at the threading on your chair there. Is that double-stitched? It looks like the heavy-duty upholstery we used to have in the breakroom at the precinct. 

Those chairs had to take a beating. Guys sitting in them with full duty belts, all that gear just grinding into the fabric day after day. A standard duty belt can weigh up to twenty pounds with the radio and the heavy flashlight and everything. My lower back is completely shot from carrying all that weight on my patrols for years. I tried going to a chiropractor once, but he just cracked my neck so hard I thought he was going to paralyze me. The spine is so fragile. It's just a stack of bones and jelly, really. If you think about it, it's a miracle we can walk upright at all. Gravity is constantly pulling us down. That's why astronauts get taller in space, you know. Without gravity, their spines decompress. I'd love to go to space, just to see the earth from up there. It must be so quiet. Just total silence. 

But... wait. I did it again, didn't I? I'm sorry, I have no idea what you just asked me.

I don't... no, I don't think so. I haven't noticed anything like that. It's kind of hard to keep track of things lately, honestly. Like time, you know? Your clock on the wall there—the second hand sweeps instead of ticks. I really appreciate that. I used to have this cheap plastic clock in my locker at the station, and the ticking would just echo inside the metal door. Drove me absolutely crazy when I was trying to come down after a graveyard shift. 

Working nights completely destroys your circadian rhythm. Your body is screaming at you to sleep, but you're out there drinking terrible gas station coffee just trying to stay alert. That coffee always tasted like burnt pennies. I actually started bringing my own thermos eventually. A big green Stanley thermos, the kind that can survive getting run over by a truck. My dad had one just like it when he worked construction. He dropped it off a three-story scaffolding once and it barely even scratched the paint. They really don't make things like that anymore, do they? Everything is just cheap plastic now, designed to break in a year so you have to buy it again. It all just ends up in a landfill. There's this documentary I saw about how much plastic is in the ocean, it's just giant floating islands of garbage... 

Wait. I'm sorry. I lost the thread again. I don't even remember what you just asked me. Did you want me to elaborate on that first part?
